title: Choosing a Database Engine
summary: Relational, key-value, document, graph, wide-column and ledger: which purpose-built database fits.
tldr: Start from the **data shape and query**: joins and transactions → relational (RDS/Aurora); key lookups at any scale → DynamoDB; JSON documents with MongoDB drivers → DocumentDB; CQL → Keyspaces; multi-hop relationships → Neptune; analytics → Redshift.
"Minimize code changes" means **match the wire protocol**: MongoDB → DocumentDB, Cassandra → Keyspaces, PostgreSQL extensions such as **PostGIS** → Aurora PostgreSQL or RDS for PostgreSQL.
Within relational, **Aurora** gives up to 15 low-lag replicas, auto-growing storage, Global Database and Serverless v2; plain **RDS** is cheaper and simpler for modest workloads.

keyFacts.text: Maximum **Aurora Replicas** per cluster, sharing the cluster storage volume so replica lag is usually well under a second.
Aurora storage keeps six copies of data across three AZs and grows automatically, with no volume to size.
**RDS Optimized Reads** puts temporary tables on instance-local NVMe storage ("d" instance classes), speeding queries that spill sorts and GROUP BYs to disk.
**Neptune** query languages. Use it for friends-of-friends, fraud rings and knowledge graphs where recursive SQL joins are too slow.
Amazon **QLDB** reached end of support in July 2025. Don't pick it for new designs; AWS points ledger workloads to Aurora PostgreSQL.

traps: DynamoDB is not a drop-in for MongoDB; switching to its API means rewriting data access code.
Aurora MySQL doesn't support PostGIS; that's a PostgreSQL extension.
Adding read replicas or bigger instances doesn't fix temp-table I/O latency; Optimized Reads does.
Running heavy analytics on the production OLTP database (or a replica of it) is the wrong answer when the question stresses TB-scale aggregations; use Redshift.
A Multi-AZ standby (non-cluster RDS) doesn't serve reads; it exists only for failover.
